---
On The Art of Paying Attention: Why Everything Becomes Interesting If You Stare At It Long Enough

There is a quiet superpower that almost no one talks about, because it doesn't look like a superpower at all. It isn't flying or telepathy or the ability to memorize pi to a thousand digits. It is the ability to find something — anything — interesting for longer than thirty seconds.

Most of us have been trained to believe that interest is a property of objects. Some things are interesting: black holes, serial killers, lost cities, celebrity breakups. Other things are boring: the toaster, the cracks in the sidewalk, the history of the zipper, the way water moves down a drain. We scroll, and scroll, and scroll, waiting for the world to do the work of interesting us.

But interest isn't in the object. It's in the attention. It's in the *quality* of the looking.

I learned this, not in a grand moment of enlightenment, but by being stuck in a laundromat in Albuquerque in August with no air conditioning and a dead phone. For forty-seven minutes, I had nothing to do but watch clothes go around. And after the initial wave of irritation and boredom passed — which took about ten minutes — something strange happened. I actually started to see it.

The clothes tumbling are not random. There is a physics to it. The drum lifts them up one side until gravity wins, and then they fall in a soft avalanche. Colors blur and then resolve. A single blue sock appears, disappears, appears again on the other side. The glass gets warm from the friction. The hum of the machine is not one note but three: a low motor drone, a higher metallic rattle, and underneath it all, the slosh of water that sounds exactly like a distant ocean. For a second I wasn't in a laundromat. I was watching a small, domesticated planet turn.

That is the whole trick. Everything is like that if you let it be.

### 1. The World is Deeper Than It Looks

We live in a world that rewards skimming. Headlines instead of articles, trailers instead of films, summaries instead of books. Skimming is efficient, but it creates an illusion: that most things are shallow.

They aren't. They are fractal.

Take something utterly mundane: a pencil.

We think a pencil is a simple object. Wood, graphite, eraser, metal thing holding the eraser on. A child understands a pencil.

But stop there and look longer.

That wood is almost always incense cedar from the Pacific Northwest, because it sharpens without splintering. That smell you get when you sharpen a pencil — that sweet, clean, slightly spicy smell — is the smell of oil in cedar heartwood. The graphite core is not graphite at all, but a baked mixture of graphite and clay, invented by Nicholas-Jacques Conte in 1795 when Napoleon's blockade cut France off from British graphite. The ratio of graphite to clay determines the hardness: more clay, harder line. That's why a 9H leaves a ghostly silver trace and a 9B leaves a soft, black smear that you can blend with your fingertip.

The little metal band that holds the eraser is called a ferrule. Before 1858, pencils didn't have erasers attached; a Philadelphia inventor named Hymen Lipman had the idea to glue one on and patented it for $100,000, which was a fortune then. The Supreme Court later invalidated his patent because, the justices wrote, it just combined two known things without inventing a new one. A bitter footnote in the history of innovation.

And the eraser itself: first made from natural rubber, now from synthetic vinyl or plasticized soy. The pink color? That's just dye. Originally to make it look more attractive. It stuck, so now we think pink *is* the color of an eraser.

All of that is inside one pencil. Now do a paperclip. Now do a spoon. Now do the window you're looking through right now. The glass in that window was made by floating molten silica on a bath of molten tin, a process invented in 1952 by Alastair Pilkington, which revolutionized architecture because for the first time humans could make perfectly flat, cheap, large panes of glass. Before that, glass had waves and bubbles and imperfections that distorted the world. Pilkington's idea meant the modern skyline could exist.

There is no boring object. There are only short attention spans.

Biologists have a term for this: *umwelt*. Coined by the ethologist Jakob von Uexküll, it means the perceptual world of an organism. A tick's umwelt is heat and butyric acid and skin. A dog's umwelt is a universe of smell layered in time. A human's umwelt is dominated by vision and language and social cues. We filter out 99.9% of what is happening to make life manageable.

But attention can widen that filter, just for a moment. The writer G.K. Chesterton put it best: “There are no uninteresting things, only uninterested people.” He meant it morally, but it's also literally true neurologically. Your brain is a prediction machine that constantly tries to tell you: *you've seen this before, move on, nothing to see here*. Boredom is not a statement about the world. It's a statement about your brain's prediction. And predictions can be wrong.

### 2. The Three Levels of Looking

After that laundromat, I started experimenting. I would deliberately pick one thing a day and look at it past the point of boredom. What I found was that looking has levels, roughly like this:

**Level One: Naming.** This is where we usually stop. You see a tree and you think “tree.” You see a bird and you think “bird, maybe a sparrow.” You have categorized it, and categorization feels like understanding. Once you've named it, your brain closes the file. Done.

This is efficient, but it's a trap. A word is not the thing. “Tree” erases the difference between a bristlecone pine that is 5,000 years old and a newly planted Bradford pear that smells like fish in the spring.

**Level Two: Noticing.** If you force yourself to stay past naming, you start to notice texture, variation, anomaly. That “tree” is not one thing. It's a vertical river of water being pulled from the roots to the leaves by transpiration, fighting gravity. Its bark has lichen on the north side. One branch is dead. Ants are farming aphids on the underside of a leaf. The wind moves through it not as a solid object but as hundreds of tiny sails adjusting independently.

At this level, the world becomes specific again. Children live here naturally; that's why they can spend twenty minutes watching an ant carry a crumb. Adults have to retrain themselves to return.

**Level Three: Connecting.** If you stay even longer — past the itch to check your phone — the object stops being isolated and starts to connect outward. That tree is connected to the sidewalk that is buckling because its roots are seeking water. That sidewalk was poured by someone in 1978. The tree is breathing out oxygen you are breathing in. It is both a living organism and an archive of weather: every ring a year of drought or rain. If it's a street tree, it was chosen by a city planner who wanted something that wouldn't drop messy fruit on cars.

Suddenly you are not looking at a tree. You are looking at botany and civil engineering and labor history and atmospheric chemistry and personal memory — because that tree smells like the one outside your childhood school.

The Japanese have a practice called *mitori keiko*, which means “learning by watching.” Apprentice sushi chefs spend years just watching the master, before they are allowed to touch the fish. Potters watch the kiln. It sounds inefficient to modern ears. But it's not. They are training the second and third levels of attention.

We don't need to apprentice for ten years to feel this. We just need to not look away so fast.

### 3. Why Boredom is Good Data

We treat boredom like a failure, like a sign that we are unstimulating people or that life is dull. We should treat it like hunger or thirst: as information.

Boredom says: *your current level of engagement is too shallow to extract meaning here.* It does not say *there is no meaning here*.

In psychology, this distinction is real. Researchers distinguish between *state boredom* — the fleeting feeling when you're stuck in a line — and *existential boredom*, a deeper disconnection. But both have the same antidote: active attention instead of passive consumption.

Passive consumption asks: *Entertain me.*
Active attention asks: *What is here that I haven't seen?*

The first puts the burden on the world. The second takes it onto yourself. And it's strangely empowering. You don't need a better movie, a better vacation, a better job to feel more alive in the next five minutes. You need a better question.

Some good questions that always work:

* What is this made of, and where did those materials come from?
* Who decided this should look like this, and what were they trying to solve?
* What is this connected to that I can't see?
* What would this look like if I were ten times smaller? A hundred times larger? A thousand years in the past?
* What is happening here that is too slow or too fast for me to perceive?

Ask any of those about a coffee mug, and you're occupied for an hour.

I'll do it now, to show you I mean it.

My mug: white ceramic, chipped on the handle. Made of kaolin clay, fired at around 1,200 degrees Celsius. Kaolin is named after Gaoling, the hill in China where it was first mined for porcelain over a thousand years ago. Europeans spent centuries trying to replicate Chinese porcelain, calling it “white gold,” failing because they didn't have the right clay. The chip on the handle happened when I washed it too quickly last Tuesday. It's now a sharp little crescent that catches the light differently — a tiny cliff where the glaze ends. The coffee inside it was grown at altitude in Colombia, shipped 2,500 miles as green beans, roasted until its sugars caramelized, ground, and brewed. The heat from the coffee is moving into my hand, into the air, eventually into the room. If I leave it long enough, a skin will form on the surface where the oils interact with oxygen — a microscopically thin membrane, boring until you remember that every skin, even on milk or coffee, is a border between two worlds, like our own skin.

You see? I didn't do anything special. I just didn't stop.

### 4. The Strange Side Effect: Awe

People chase awe in big places: the Grand Canyon, the Northern Lights, a cathedral. But awe doesn't require bigness. It requires *perceived vastness* and a need to mentally accommodate it. Psychologists Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt, who have spent decades studying awe, found that it has two ingredients: something feels vast, and your current mental model can't quite hold it.

A galaxy is vast. But so is the number of interactions happening inside a single cell. So is the age of that bristlecone pine. So is the chain of human hands — farmer, picker, shipper, roaster, packer, driver, cashier — that got these coffee grounds into my kitchen.

When you look long enough, small things become vast, because they open onto networks and histories and scales that dwarf you. That's why paying attention feels, after a while, almost spiritual, even if you are not a spiritual person. The world *is* overwhelming. We just keep our blinders on to get through the day.

There is a wonderful term from the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins: *inscape*. He meant the unique inner essence of a thing — the “thisness” of this oak, this river, this face, that makes it unlike any other. Hopkins, who was a Jesuit priest, believed inscape revealed the divine. You don't need to believe that to use the word. You just need to have felt that there is something irreducible about a specific thing that a category never captures. The way your best friend laughs. The exact blue of October sky at 4 p.m. The inscape of a single, well-worn shoe.

Attention is how you get to inscape.

### 5. How to Practice, Without Making It a Chore

I don't want this to sound like homework. The world does not need another productivity hack. So here is a very unserious, low-pressure way to play with this:

1. **The One-Thing Rule.** Once a day, pick one thing you would normally ignore and give it 60 seconds of real attention. The doorknob. The sound of the refrigerator. The shadow on the wall. No need to write a poem about it. Just look, or listen, until the boredom wave passes. Notice what happens on the other side of it.

2. **Copy a Child.** Children tap, shake, smell, lick — they use all their senses. Adults privilege vision. Next time you can do so safely, pick something up and feel its weight and temperature. Smell it. A fresh paperback smells like volatile organic compounds off-gassing from ink and adhesive. A rock warmed by the sun smells faintly metallic. Your nose knows more than you let it.

3. **Follow One Thread.** Choose a thing and follow it backwards one step. Your T-shirt: who sewed it? Your breakfast banana: how did it get here still yellow? (Answer: they are picked green and gassed with ethylene). The cracks in your ceiling: why there and not elsewhere? You don't need to become an expert. Just pulling one thread shows you how knotted everything is.

4. **Be Bored on Purpose.** Next time you are waiting — in line, on hold, for water to boil — don't fill the gap. Don't pull out your phone for ten seconds longer than is comfortable. Let your eyes wander and land somewhere. Attention, like a shy animal, shows up when you're still.

None of this will make your life perfect. There are forms of suffering that attention alone can't fix. And there are times when distraction is exactly what you need — to rest, to recover, to not feel everything at once. This is not about being mindful every second. It's about remembering you have the option.

The laundromat in Albuquerque is gone now, I think. I drove past that lot last year and there was a different building there, a dollar store. But I still remember the blue sock going around, and the way the sun through the dirty window made the dust visible, each mote a tiny planet in orbit around nothing in particular, until the air conditioner kicked on and scattered them.

Everything is like that. The whole world is a laundromat if you have a minute.

And if you are alive and reading this, you do.

You have a minute. You have, if you're lucky, many, many minutes strung together into years. You can spend them waiting to be interested. Or you can walk outside, look at whatever is in front of you — the gutter, the pigeon, the half-dead houseplant you forgot to water — and decide to be interested on purpose.

The plant is trying to tell you something, by the way. Its leaves are drooping not from sadness but from turgor pressure dropping as water leaves its cells. And that yellowing lower leaf? It's reabsorbing its own chlorophyll to survive, cannibalizing itself to keep growing toward whatever light you've given it. That's not a failure. That's resilience with no audience.

Pay attention. It's all paying you back, just by being there, waiting to be seen past its name.

---

The recurring moral claim is that looking closely can make life feel more alive, with an explicit qualification that distraction and rest also have their place.

> Everything is like that if you let it be.

Medium: the essay sustains a coherent, recurring commitment to curiosity and ordinary wonder, though its polished advice-essay structure makes that commitment less individually distinctive.
